extracted.intended_audience: aspiring orators and students of rhetoric (classical/public speaking)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and delivering classical eloquence: what a complete orator must know, how to train, which styles to use, and how to adapt tone and delivery to audience and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy as foundation of Eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: The eloquent Speaker we are enquiring after, cannot be formed without the assistance of Philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy supplies the materials and methods of reasoning: discovering genus and species, just definitions, analysis of parts, distinguishing true from false, foreseeing consequences, dissolving ambiguities, and understanding natural philosophy and moral principles which furnish the richest treasures of elocution. Examples cited: Pericles learned from Anaxagoras; Demosthenes attended Plato's lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive liberal education (literature, law, history, philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator should possess a wide acquaintance with literature, be nurtured in Philosophy, have an accurate knowledge of the Civil Law, and be a complete master of Roman History.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This body of learning enables appeals to venerable evidence, informed management of private causes, and supplies 'the furniture of philosophical Science' to enrich Oratory. The text lists additional practical abilities tied to learning: entangling opponents humorously, dilating and expanding subject-matter, enlivening by digression, rousing indignation or compassion, and influencing the judge's soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous practice and composition (writing as training)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvement of eloquence requires continual practice, notably the exercise of writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's practice: studying under masters, long apprenticeship pleading causes, and persistent writing produced improvements (abated vehemence, corrected ardour, strengthened lungs). Teachers such as Molo disciplined youthful luxuriancy. Writing is singled out as particularly beneficial among exercises for refining style and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical delivery: voice, action, and carriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Good oratory requires training of voice, action, and physical carriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices strengthen lungs, moderate vehemence of voice and gesture, and secure a graceful carriage analogous to how the Palaestra trains an Actor's bodily carriage. Physical delivery is a necessary accomplishment of a good Actor and thus of an effective public speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt to audience taste and local style
rubrics_metrics.description: The taste of the Audience governs and directs the Eloquence of the Speaker; one must accommodate to the humours and dispositions of those who hear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional examples: inhabitants of Caria, Phrygia, Mysia prefer luxuriant/corpulent style; Rhodians and Greeks dislike it; Athenians demand correctness and elegance. Anti-pattern: using Asiatic luxuriancy before an Athenian audience would provoke rejection. Choose style to suit the audience's critical ear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish and master the three kinds of Eloquence (lofty, simple, middle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good speaking may be divided into three characters: the lofty and majestic; the simple and easy; and a middle kind that mixes the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lofty/majestic: impetuous, copious, weighty, able to alarm and sway passions (may be harsh or smooth). Simple/easy: aims chiefly at information, clear and neat, sometimes purposely unpolished as an artificer’s tactic or else elegant and facetious. Middle: blends both without excelling; smooth and equable. A consummate orator would master all three and use them appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atticism: correctness, clarity, and appropriate ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: True Atticism is not merely plainness; it may be plain and simple but can also be florid, nervous, and copious — provided it is correct and not faulty or impertinent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lysias exemplifies Attic politeness and correctness; Demosthenes is held up as the ideal Attic model (complete Attic Speaker). Warning: some who call themselves Attic mistake plain, unornamented speech for the whole of Atticism. Attic taste cares for accuracy and elegant expression; ornament must not be faulty or impertinent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and intelligibility; avoid obscure, intricate periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Public discourse must be intelligible; obscure and intricate periods are the greatest fault an Orator can commit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thucydides' manner (obscure, intricate periods suitable to a historian) is inappropriate for the Forum. The orator must favor clarity so that the public can follow the argument; avoid treating public discourse like historiography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate ornamentation and restraint; avoid luxuriancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Repress the luxuriancy of juvenile imagination and avoid ornate turns of sentiment that are delicate and entertaining but not useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Molo's instruction was to restrain youthful luxuriancy. Hortensius and others showed brilliant, rapid, and ornamental language that pleased the young and the populace but lost weight and dignity with age. Avoid showy, superficial ornaments that lack substance; ornamental expression can be ridiculed when attention fades (Aeschines mocked Demosthenes’ singular expressions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform style to age and station
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain styles (e.g., Asiatic) are more allowable in a young man than in an old one; one must change manner as dignity and years require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hortensius excelled in youthful Asiatic-style ornament and rapidity but later it became unbecoming; honours and age require more gravity and composure. Failure to adapt will make a speaker less pleasing in later life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic progression of argument and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose the discourse with a deliberate progression: begin coolly and modestly, increase argumentative pressure and poignancy, and warm the passions toward the close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demosthenes' oration for Ctesiphon is cited as exemplary: he sets out modestly, grows more pressing when arguing law, and ultimately exults as he warms the judges’ passions. Structure tone to lead the audience from calm reasoning to stronger emotional appeal as suits the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic reasoning and precision (definitions, analysis, anticipating objections)
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of reasoning is essential: define things justly, analyze their parts, distinguish truth from falsehood, foresee consequences, point out inconsistencies, and dissolve ambiguities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without philosophical instruction, an orator cannot perform these analytic tasks. These skills support clear legal and moral argumentation and prevent being confounded by subtle objections or ambiguities in cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid harsh, rough, or disharmonious delivery without measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Some try to affect energy by harsh, rough, gloomy speaking without harmony or measure — a flawed means of producing force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Energy can be produced either by a harsh rough style or by a smooth, regular, well-proportioned style; the former lacks harmony and is a defect unless checked by proportion and rhetorical skill. Favor harmony and measured force over untempered harshness.
